must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2c81ff3c50013c149dc6a5db67bbe11cccdbbef22ce2c0712101f4a358bcb8c.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{2t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{2t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{t})^{′}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}}{{c}_{1}{e}^{t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2c81ff3c50013c149dc6a5db67bbe11cccdbbef22ce2c0712101f4a358bcb8c.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{2t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{2t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{t})^{′}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}}{{c}_{1}{e}^{t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2c81ff3c50013c149dc6a5db67bbe11cccdbbef22ce2c0712101f4a358bcb8c.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{2t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{2t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{t})^{′}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}}{{c}_{1}{e}^{t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186305099 :question/id #uuid "f20c0d44-466d-592f-adfd-5535d1164b77" :question/math-academy-id "q-332705"} {:db/id 17592186305100 :question/id #uuid $$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=9$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{9t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{9t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{9t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/99/99d6e9894c7117c5684e17702540d0eb469b6e824381cf2263c843f8f55ee8d8.png)

$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.$ 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/75/75e7a0e16141db2a8da210c1ab30fc7328ccc98f861afec4db69d951ff3c9121.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/28/280e99a308962d43d1060be7100e294623d3bc3bfbe0579ab61d817695ad9e45.svg) Since $\lambda_2>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

Because both axes are *unstable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called an **unstable node** or **source**.

In the phase portrait, we draw:

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), and

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin).

A typical trajectory for an *unstable node* emanates from the origin toward infinity.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).
